Hi all,

During Community over Code in Glasgow, we discussed authentication in
Iceberg REST and concluded that we should downscope the OAuth2
AuthManager v2 initiative.

The general feedback was that v2 contains too much new surface at
once, especially grant types. Support for complex legacy behavior
(e.g. vended tokens) also unnecessarily clutters the implementation,
and some people suggested dropping that as well.

I therefore propose to reboot the initiative, with a much smaller scope in mind:

- One single grant: client_credentials.
- Two client authentication methods: client_secret_basic and client_secret_post.
- Simplified token renewal (by re-running the grant before expiry).
- Reduced support for legacy v1 (migrate common properties, but leave
the rest out).

The above scope fits in one PR, so here it is:

https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18756

I truly hope we can get this released in Iceberg 1.13, so that users
can finally benefit from a standards-complaint OAuth2 manager in
Iceberg REST.

Let me know your thoughts.

Thanks,
Alex

body:
Hi all,

Following up on the "should V4 manifests be Parquet-only?" thread [1], I'd
like to continue the discussion here about supporting various data file
formats in V4.

*Should we stop writing new ORC and Avro data files in V4?* Note that this
would only affect new writes; existing ORC and Avro files in upgraded
tables would still be readable.

I've been thinking about this in two dimensions, with more details at the
end of the email.

Feature gaps:
ORC and Avro don't fully support some of the features we've been adding,
and our own format TCK already lists what each one is missing [2]. For
example, neither supports variant shredding, and the current draft of the
vector type spec doesn't support ORC. This also came up last year in #13060
[3] which proposed validating file format compatibility for V3 tables.

Upstream activity:
Both projects are maintained, but there's limited activity on the formats
themselves. The last format changes we needed actually came from folks from
the Iceberg community: Gang added geo types to ORC, and Fokko added
nanosecond timestamps and fixed-size UUIDs to Avro. Otherwise, the features
we need aren't being worked on, so I don't expect these gaps to close on
their own.

At a high level, the questions for the community are:

   1. Should we stop writing new ORC and Avro data files in V4?
   2. What does it mean for Iceberg to support ORC and Avro in V4? If we
   keep them, are we okay with users not being able to use some V4 features
   with them, as is already the case in V3?
   3. If we stop writing them, what bar should a format meet to be writable
   again in a future version?
   4. Are there any users of ORC or Avro data files today? What are your
   thoughts about using these in V4 versus Parquet?

I'd love to hear your thoughts!

Best,
Kevin Liu

[1] https://lists.apache.org/thread/fym02576n5sqy298fjxl0xmsv9z5rb7y
[2]
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/6951360ec8a01644d3c24824ab635e06a82f8a7c/data/src/test/java/org/apache/iceberg/data/ReadFormatModelTests.java#L190-L212
[3] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13060
[4] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/18386
[5] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18387
[6] https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#appendix-a-format-specific-requirements
[7]
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/6951360ec8a01644d3c24824ab635e06a82f8a7c/orc/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/orc/ORC.java#L114-L117
[8] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18416/files
[9]
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/6951360ec8a01644d3c24824ab635e06a82f8a7c/core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/avro/AvroMetrics.java#L35
[10] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17119
[11] https://lists.apache.org/list?[email removed]:lte=1y:
[12] https://github.com/apache/orc-format/commits/main/specification
[13] https://lists.apache.org/list?[email removed]:lte=1y:
[14] https://lists.apache.org/thread/ds0gm18b8cghotv4xtsmgo2ybghht60m
[15]
https://github.com/apache/avro/commits/main/doc/content/en/docs/++version++/Specification/_index.md
[16] https://lists.apache.org/list?[email removed]:lte=1y:
[17] https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/commits/master
[18] https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/pull/624

*More details*

Feature gaps that block a V3 feature or a proposed V4 feature:

   - ORC
      - Default values (V3): our integration can't read them [2]
      - Geometry and geography types (V3): our integration can't read or
      write them [2]
      - Variant type (V3): writes currently fail in Spark [4], and the
      pending fix only turns the crash into a clear error [5]
      - Variant shredding (V3): not supported, per the spec [6], so we
      don't produce variant bounds for ORC files either
      - Table encryption (V3): our integration rejects the encrypted files
      that table encryption produces, so ORC can't be used in
encrypted tables [7]
      - Vector type (proposed for V4): marked as not supported in the
      current draft of the vector type spec [8]
   - Avro
      - Variant shredding (V3): not supported, per the spec [6], so we
      don't produce variant bounds for Avro files either
      - Geo bounds (V3): Avro can store geo types, but the Avro data files
      we write have no column metrics (there's been a TODO for this since 2021
      [9]), so they don't carry the bounding boxes used for pruning
   - #13060 noted in May 2025 that "Parquet is currently the only file
   format that supports all the required capabilities for v3 compatibility"
   [3]. It was approved but never merged, and Avro has since closed some of
   those gaps, such as geo types [10].

Upstream activity in the last 12 months:

   - ORC
      - Dev list: no technical discussions, only release votes and admin
      threads [11]
      - Format spec: unchanged since Gang added geo types in April 2025 [12]
   - Avro
      - Dev list: the technical threads were about the language SDKs, not
      the format [13]. The only two questions about the format itself got no
      replies, including one about standardizing a vector type that came out of
      our vector work [14]
      - Format spec: unchanged since December 2024. The last
      Iceberg-related changes were Fokko's nanosecond timestamps (Dec 2023) and
      fixed-size UUIDs (Jan 2024) [15]
   - Parquet
      - Dev list: roughly 100 technical threads [16]
      - Format spec: added a FILE type, ALP encoding (in preview), and NaN
      counts [17], and a vector type is being discussed [18]

body:
Hey folks!

I've been working on a proposal aimed at enabling an ecosystem of Puffin
blob types, with opinionated (but hopefully lightweight) metadata about
configuration, scope, and how future blobs interact with deletion and
compaction.

For context, separate from any Iceberg specifics, I've been daydreaming
about an idea of "progressive indexing" for a few years: after a file is
written, perhaps weeks or months later, we may discover that read workloads
could be much faster and/or more efficient if we'd made different indexing
choices before. Unfortunately, it's hard to predict whether any such change
might impact ingest workloads, and rewriting data, while commonplace on
small files during early compaction eras, is a non-starter for files that
are large and old, so some read-heavy workloads are stuck with scanning
huge volumes of data that often has high-selectivity features lurking in
dusty corners.

While building out an early, as yet unpublished version of the progressive
indexing idea, I realized that while I was initially focused on the
_timing_ of index builds (still important!) I hadn't spent enough time on
the _diversity_ of available indexes, and how to rein in the predictable
chaos if my earlier goals were achieved and such choices became broadly
available.

So, in recent days, this proposal has evolved to focus on what I now
consider a prerequisite for the timing and diversity visions, which is: how
do we construct and operate an ecosystem that would support the desired
diversity, within guardrails that make the chaos less likely and more
contained, in which query accuracy can be safeguarded as long as
implementers play by the rules?

I have looked at the parallel v4 proposal for secondary indexes, and I
believe my proposal is complementary, even though there are significant
overlaps in scope. In particular mine focuses mainly (but not exclusively)
on filters, or "negative" indices, in which an out-of-date index merely
costs efficiency (i.e. a file/chunk that does not contain rows that satisfy
the predicate is scanned), whereas the `scalar` index described in the v4
proposal is a "positive" index, in which much more care is required to
prevent mutations from corrupting indexes, which would cause query
correctness problems. Section 12 of my proposal is a detailed comparison.

This email is already long enough, so rather than go into further detail,
I'll ask you to have a look at
https://github.com/acruise/iceberg-indexing-ecosystem/blob/main/docs/proposals/puffin-blob-types-and-compaction.md
which is admittedly far too long, just like this email!

Hi all,

The spec is ambiguous about Parquet data files that carry field IDs for
some fields but not all, and no two of the four implementations I checked
resolve such a file the same way. I'd like to agree on one reading and
write it into the spec.

Column Projection [1] says a reader should "use schema.name-mapping.default
metadata to map field id to columns without field id", which reads as per
column. The paragraph that follows says the mappings "provide fallback
field ids to be used when a data file does not contain field id
information", which reads as per file. For a file with no IDs at all, both
readings agree. They diverge when only some fields carry an ID.

What the readers do today, on their main branches:

- Java (ReadConf, ParquetSchemaUtil.HasIds): if any field in the file has
an ID, the file is resolved by ID only and the name mapping is not
consulted.
- PyIceberg (pyarrow_to_schema, _HasIds): IDs are used only if every field,
including list elements and map keys and values, has one; otherwise the
whole file is resolved through the name mapping.
- iceberg-rust (arrow/reader/pipeline.rs): the first top-level column
decides; if it has an ID, the file is resolved by ID only.
- iceberg-go (table/internal/parquet_files.go, pruneParquetSchema.fieldID):
Parquet column pruning resolves per field; an embedded ID wins, and the
mapping fills in the fields without one.

This happens in practice. Delta tables with column mapping, written without
IcebergCompatV2, store IDs for top-level columns but none for map keys and
values or list elements. When such a table gets Iceberg metadata [2],
PyIceberg reads the map columns through the name mapping, while the Java
reader resolves by ID only and does not find the map's key and value. The
same table gives different results depending on the reader.

I propose the per-field reading, which matches the Column Projection rule:
a field with an embedded ID is resolved by that ID, and a field without one
falls back to the name mapping. It never overrides an ID a writer recorded,
it changes nothing for files with full IDs or with none, and it makes the
partial case readable.

If there is agreement, I can open a spec PR that clarifies the paragraph,
and contribute a fixture to iceberg-verification [3]: a file with IDs on
its top-level fields only, as a companion to the base name-mapping table
that issue covers.

Is there a reason for the per-file behaviour that I'm missing, for example
a correctness concern with mixing ID and name resolution within one file?

[1]
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/%23column-projection&source=gmail&ust=1793746430284000&sa=E
[2]
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://github.com/apache/incubator-xtable/issues/911&source=gmail&ust=1793746430284000&sa=E
[3]
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://github.com/apache/iceberg-verification/issues/14&source=gmail&ust=1793746430284000&sa=E

Thanks,
Sylwester

Hi all,

I'm a contributor to Apache Polaris. We have a question about the REST
catalog's metrics endpoint (POST
/v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}/metrics, reportMetrics)
that we'd like to settle with the Iceberg community before changing server
behavior.

*Background*

Polaris can persist metrics reports sent to this endpoint. Today, if the
database write fails, the endpoint returns a 500. A pending Polaris PR [1]
would log the failure, increment a drop counter, and return 204 instead.
The motivation is that a degraded metrics store shouldn't show up as a
catalog failure. The discussion on the Polaris dev list [2] has split on
this.

*What the spec says*
The spec defines the operation as "Send a metrics report to this endpoint
to be processed by the backend". It documents 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 419,
503 and 5XX. It doesn't say whether reporting is best-effort or whether a
catalog must signal a failure to process a report. It also doesn't say what
a client should do on a 5xx.

*What clients do*

As far as I know, the Java client's REST metrics reporter catches and logs
errors from this endpoint and does not retry. I haven't checked the other
implementations (PyIceberg, iceberg-rust, iceberg-go), so please correct me.

*The two readings*

*1. Best-effort telemetry.* The client sends the report and moves on. A
catalog may drop a report it can't persist, as long as it surfaces that to
operators. A 5xx tells the client nothing it can act on.

*2. A normal REST write.* If the catalog can't process the report, it says
so with a 5xx, and clients may retry. This matters for anyone using the
reports for auditing or billing, though it only helps if clients actually
retry.

*Questions*

1. Is reportMetrics intended to be best-effort? Is a catalog allowed to
accept a report and discard it, or fail to process it, without signaling
failure?
2. If a catalog can't process a report, what should it return? Is 5xx the
expected answer, or is 204 acceptable?
3. Should clients be expected to retry a failed report? If so, the spec
should say that. If not, it should say reporting is not guaranteed delivery.
4. Should the spec state any of this in the endpoint description, so
implementations behave consistently?

We'd like to follow whatever the community decides rather than invent
Polaris-specific behavior. I'm happy to send a spec PR with clarifying
wording once there's a direction.

Thanks,
Anand

[1] https://github.com/apache/polaris/pull/5395
[2] https://lists.apache.org/thread/0r7fpq153d2ny0tbt162051dh0jv3wjb

The metrics endpoint and metrics reporting is intended to be best-effort
and the RESTMetricsReporter implementation also ensures it does not bubble
up any errors.
I don't think we want reads/writes to fail just because the server couldn't
store information about the scan/commit.

endpoint because those are all potential errors. It is up to the catalog
implementation to decide whether to throw a 500 or just log an error. The
catalog can also decide to discard metrics reports and return 204.

overall duration of a scan/commit and we don't want to negatively affect
the read/write path.

I don't think we need to explicitly define the behavior as best effort in
the spec.  The endpoint has defined behavior and return codes.  It being
separate from a commit inherently makes it a separate operation
disconnected from the commit itself.  The idea of "best effort" is probably
misleading here.  The critical operation is the commit.  Metrics are
separate and reporting is not required for the commit.

reasonable for the server to return a code that doesn't represent what
actually happened within the request.  Returning a success code when
there's a failure is clearly wrong and an implementation issue.  However,
whether a client retries or ignores the failure response from the metrics
endpoint is a client-side implementation issue.

I played with Steve's suggestion, and I think it's the right
direction. Here are the main ideas:

Hi Dan and Russell,

A proposal to close the API question: replace catalogName(String) with
hadoopConf(Configuration), with Dan's FileIO lookup as the default. I agree
with Russell that catalogName does not say what it controls.

   - hadoopConf(Configuration) on DeleteOrphanFilesSparkAction is the
   Hadoop configuration the listing uses, replacing the session configuration
   when set. RemoveOrphanFilesProcedure passes the session configuration plus
   the spark.sql.catalog.<name>.hadoop.* overrides of the catalog it was
   invoked on, which is what SparkUtil.hadoopConfCatalogOverrides already
   builds for SparkCatalog. The action keeps wrapping it in
   SerializableConfiguration and no longer knows about Spark catalog names.
   - Default, per Dan's suggestion: when hadoopConf is not set and table.io()
   is HadoopConfigurable, use the configuration it holds; otherwise the
   session configuration as today. For tables loaded through SparkCatalog that
   is the session configuration plus the catalog's hadoop.* overrides, so
   HadoopFileIO and ResolvingFileIO users get the fix without calling
   anything. This reads the configuration the FileIO was built with, so there
   is no name-based catalog lookup and no catalog loading side effect,
   which is what the PR review rejected. It is a change from what I said on
   the PR, that nothing changes without opting in; I think it is the right
   default since it is the configuration the table already reads and writes
   with. Say so if you would rather keep it opt-in.

It is still one public method, on the Spark action only, not on the
DeleteOrphanFiles interface. The procedure is in a different package, so it
has to be public. Going through the generic option(...) map was discussed
in the PR review and set aside as the same thing stringly typed, and the
action already takes an arbitrary location, so a typed setter for the
configuration it lists with adds no new capability.

The default alone does not cover #17860: as in my last reply, S3FileIO,
GCSFileIO and ADLSFileIO are not HadoopConfigurable, so the listing would
still use the session configuration and fail with AccessDenied. The
spark.sql.catalog.<name>.hadoop.* overrides are the only per-catalog place
a user can configure the Hadoop FileSystem the listing uses, so the
procedure passes them. As agreed in the review, the fix stays limited to
those explicit overrides; hadoopConfCatalogOverrides keeps its contract and
the action does no credential derivation. prefix_listing does authenticate
through table.io(), but it lists serially on the driver into a single
partition (#16932, #17387), so it is not a drop-in for large tables; making
it parallel is a separate change.

Does this shape work for you? If so, or if there are no objections by the
end of next week (November 15th), I will push it to #17862 this week,
retarget the PR to the 4.2 module, ask yangshangqing95 to re-review since
his approval was on the catalogName shape, and follow with the 4.1, 4.0 and
3.5 backports. The action tests move from catalogName to hadoopConf, plus
one for the default path on a HadoopConfigurable FileIO, and
spark-procedures.md gets the default rule. If you would rather see
something else, a pointer before I rework it would help.

Thanks,
Sebastian

Hi Russell,

Point 2 of my earlier reply does work for HadoopFileIO and ResolvingFileIO,
agreed. So the shape would be: when table.io() is HadoopConfigurable the
listing uses its configuration; otherwise, it uses the session
configuration as today.

What it does not fix is the case in #17860 itself. For Glue the default
FileIO is S3FileIO, and S3FileIO, GCSFileIO and ADLSFileIO are not
HadoopConfigurable. A stock Glue catalog with a cross-account role
therefore still lists with the cluster identity after this change and still
gets AccessDenied. The user has three ways out: io-impl set to
ResolvingFileIO, io-impl set to HadoopFileIO, or prefix_listing. The first
keeps S3FileIO underneath and only borrows the Hadoop configuration for the
listing:

spark.sql.catalog.tenant.io-impl org.apache.iceberg.io.ResolvingFileIO
spark.sql.catalog.tenant.client.factory
org.apache.iceberg.aws.AssumeRoleAwsClientFactory
spark.sql.catalog.tenant.client.assume-role.arn
arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/lakehouse-access
spark.sql.catalog.tenant.hadoop.fs.s3a.aws.credentials.provider
org.apache.hadoop.fs.s3a.auth.AssumedRoleCredentialProvider
spark.sql.catalog.tenant.hadoop.fs.s3a.assumed.role.arn
arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/lakehouse-access
spark.sql.catalog.tenant.hadoop.fs.s3a.assumed.role.credentials.provider
com.amazonaws.auth.WebIdentityTokenCredentialsProvider

It works, but it asks the user to change their FileIO to fix a maintenance
procedure, and to declare the role twice because the listing authenticates
through s3a while everything else goes through the SDK.

The second option, HadoopFileIO with the same hadoop.* keys, puts listing
and table I/O on one identity path, but every read, write and delete then
goes through s3a instead of S3FileIO: deletes drop from DeleteObjects
batches of up to 1000 keys to one call per file, and the s3.* catalog
properties stop applying. A fallback, not the IO the AWS docs recommend.

The third option, prefix_listing, is the right path for a non-Hadoop IO,
but today it lists serially on the driver into a single partition (#16932,
#17387), and on Spark Connect that also runs into
spark.rpc.message.maxSize, which a client session cannot raise. So for
S3FileIO users the correct path does not scale and the scalable path has
the wrong credentials.

Two possible follow-ups, and I would like a steer on which fits:

1. Make ResolvingFileIO the default FileIO for the Glue catalog, as it
already is for REST. For s3:// locations it delegates to S3FileIO with the
same properties, so the data path is unchanged, but table.io() becomes
HadoopConfigurable and the stock Glue case is covered by the shape above.
The catch is that ResolvingFileIO needs Hadoop on the classpath, which the
AWS module does not require today, so that is a question for the AWS
maintainers.

2. A parallel prefix listing on the executors, so that prefix_listing gives
S3FileIO users the same scalability as the Hadoop walk, with the table's
own credentials and no s3a configuration at all.

If the HadoopConfigurable shape is what you want for #17862, I will rework
it against the 4.2 module and follow with the 4.1, 4.0 and 3.5 backports.

Thanks,
Sebastian

Thanks, Russell, for your time on this, I'll try my best to explain.

If you select GlueCatalog as IcebergCatalog and no io-impl, by default you
get S3FileIO as io-impl (
https://iceberg.apache.org/docs/1.5.1/aws/#s3-fileio).
Now, if you have Spark running in AWS Account A with a base IAM Role A (say
IRSA or Pod Identity), and the lakehouse (Glue + S3) in AWS Account B, and
you need to chain assume IAM role B from A to access data in account B
(think of a multitenant setting), everything works
except remove_orphan_files as it will still use IAM Role A (and fail with
access denied - this is the bug we want to solve).

Right now, the DeleteOrphanFilesSparkAction constructor
<https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/5329317ad465d81dd940768d6c6b903044e58935/spark/v4.2/spark/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/spark/actions/DeleteOrphanFilesSparkAction.java#L136>
takes
a SparkSession object and a Table object, and initializes hadoopConf as new
SerializableConfiguration(spark.sessionState().newHadoopConf()).
newHadoopConf()
only sees spark.hadoop.* properties, dropping the catalog. This is why it
ends up using IAM role A.

In my PR I added a public `catalogName` method
to DeleteOrphanFilesSparkAction and changed the hadoopConf property to
non-final so that one could figure out the correct hadoopConf tied to the
catalog. Daniel suggested extracting the hadoopConf from Table.io()
instead, thus avoiding changes to the class's public interface. However,
this would only work if the FileIO implementation (io-impl) is
either HadoopFileIO or ResolvingFileIO. As I said, by default it is
S3FileIO, which has no hadoopConf.

So a user needs to know that, when configuring a Glue catalog with
cross-account access, they also need to change the io-impl to ResolvingFileIO
just so that remove_orphan_files works correctly.

Hi Alex,

I'm +1 generally speaking. Also, I think it's a good idea to hide Jackson
behind Iceberg types, it's a good cleanup (not directly related to Jackson
3).

Reading your points, I have a few comments:
1. About the ordering and "mixing" Jackson 2 and 3, I would do the shims
first (your items 3 and 4) while they are still backed by Jackson 2. We
could deprecate the Jackson typed API in 1.13 (I'm thinking especially
HTTPRequest.mapper() and HTTPClient.Builder.withObjectMapper()). The switch
to Jackson 3 then becomes an internal change, and we ship both Jackson 2
and 3 for a short time. Bundling both is not really a technical problem:
they use different packages, and the Spark/Flink runtime jars already
relocate com.fasterxml, so we just need a tools.jackson relocation. It just
makes the jar bigger and more "exposed" (CVE, etc).
2. Rather than writing new tests, I would parameterize the existing parser
tests (TestSchemaParser, REST request/response parser tests, ...) to run
against both Jackson 2 and Jackson 3 during the transition, They already
cover the JSON contracts. Also, comparing the serialized output of Jackson
2 & 3 would also catch the default feature changes in Jackson 3.
3. I would be very very careful on your point 4, about the REST layer. REST
catalog servers register the serializers on the ObjectMapper. Polaris, for
instance, does that with Quarkus mapper, and Quarkus is moving to Jackson
3. These servers can't avoid Jackson completely: they need a Jackson module
to plug into their mapper. Also, RESTSerializers exposes about 20 public
nested serializer/deserializer classes that extend Jackson types, not only
registerAll(). So I don't think shims alone are enough here. The "separate
artifacts" idea from your first email (and Steve legacy module) fits this
part well. Core would stay binding agnostic, and small adapter modules
(something like iceberg-rest-jackson2 and iceberg-rest-jackson3) would each
expose a Jackson module. Servers pick the one they need.
4. I agree with the splitting. I would suggest:
- introduce the shims and migrate the parsers package by package (several
PRs, I would be happy to help there)
- the REST layer
- dual binding tests and Jackson 3 switch
- removal of the deprecated Jackson 2

Happy to help there!

Regards
JB

Hi Roman,

I think it's a good idea to clarify this.

I checked the Java side. DateTimeUtil.nanosToMicros has used Math.floorDiv
since timestamp_ns / timestamptz_ns were first added, and Bucket hashes
that result. I also recomputed the example: hashing -1 µs gives bucket[100]
= 12, and hashing 0 µs gives 76. So floor division is what the reference
impl has always done. Since Java, Go and Rust (now) all agree, I see this
as a clarification of existing behavior, not a format change.

I have a couple of suggestions on the PR (I will cast there too):
- Put the rounding rule straight into note 3 so all the conversion
requirements stay in one place, something like "Nanosecond timestamps must
be converted to microsecond precision before hashing, by dividing by 1,000
and rouding toward negative infinity (floor division) to ensure timestamps
have the same hash value".
- Add a pre epoch test value to the timestamp_ns and timestamptz_ns rows,
for example 1969-12-31T23:59:59.999999999 ￫ 1651860712 (that's
hashLong(-1)). Truncate toward zero would give 1669671676 instead, so the
table itself would catch any implementation that gets this wrong.

I will review the PR.

Thanks!

body:
Hi guys,

Thanks for bumping this thread (I just saw that thanks to Dan :)).

I agree with Dan: authorization should drive the request shape, and it's
easier to settle it now.

A few thoughts:
- If the server needs context to authorize a FILE reference, it has to be
per element, as a batch can span several data files and columns. I would
keep the top level properties as it is and add an optional context on
RemoteSignBatchElement. Mixing client provided context with server provided
static properties in the same map would be confusing imho.
- If servers rely on this context to autorize, all clients (Java, Python,
Rust, ...) have to send the same thing, so I think it should be defined in
the spec (for instance data file location and field ID) and not as opaque
keys in a map. I would also use the field ID rather than the column name:
names change on rename and are ambiguous for nested fields.
- The context is a claim from the client. The server can check that the
caller has access to the column (and maybe that the data file is part of
the table), but it can't verify that the URI is actually referenced in that
file without reading it. So for shared storage, the server still needs its
own control (for instance allowed locations for a FILE column), and the
spec should be clear that the context helps the decision but is not a proof
by itself. On the cost side, elements sharing the same (data file, field
ID) can be authorized once, so the cost scales with the number of distinct
pairs, not with the number of rows.

Per element authorization also answers the partial results question from
the PR review: with shared storage, some elements of a batch can be signed
while others are denied, so the completed/failed split makes sense.

I’m also not sure to standardize AI functions in the Iceberg expression
spec. The spec deliberately defines a small, engine-neutral expression
model, with common predicates and a limited set of portable functions
closely tied to Iceberg’s needs (ie, data organization and skipping). It

adoption easier.

require agreement on semantics such as model identity, versioning,
inference configuration, and determinism. I’d prefer to use the existing
function/UDF mechanisms unless there is a clear Iceberg-specific need for a
standardized contract.

Hi JB and Dan,

Thanks for the reviews. I agree we should be clear on how authorization for the FILE type works for a REST catalog server, and that the interface supports those semantics.

The initial batch api proposal assumes, like the existing access delegation endpoints, that the server authorizes the request's principal against the table.

Regarding Dan's point on including more granular auth context into the request: since an external FILE reference originates from a column in a data file, I can see why we'd want that context to be in the authorization input. I think JB made some great observations on this topic:

1. The context would be an optional, spec-defined input (data file location and field ID), kept separate from the server-provided `properties`.
2. Use field-id over column names
3. It is a claim from the client. It informs the server's decision but is not proof, so for shared storage the server still needs its own control and verification.

Because the context is optional, adding it later does not change the behavior of clients and servers that don't use it, and a server that needs it can refuse requests without it. So I think we can treat it as an enhancement rather than block the batch API on it.

I think where the context lives is still an open question. JB makes a good case for defining it at the element level in `RemoteSignBatchElement`, since a batch can span several data files and FILE columns. But keeping it at `RemoteSignBatchRequest` would keep elements smaller, at the cost of clients grouping by data file and field.
Either way we could add it as an optional context, and if we do support it, I think it's also worth considering the feature across other access delegation modes (like vended credentials).

That's my thought on this specific requirement. But that being said, I'm happy to keep this thread open while the FILE implementation settles, so we capture authorization semantics we haven't thought of yet.

Here is a summary of yesterday's index sync. Thanks to everyone who joined.

1. Derived columns
Péter asked whether derived columns (for example, storing Hilbert values in
the index) should be index-only or part of the table spec, and whether in
V4 or V5.

   columns will move forward in parallel, as a separate effort building on the
   existing derived columns proposal.

   derived columns reach consensus, the index spec picks them up through the
   shared schema.

2. Index REST spec (#16963)
Agreed:

   - Nest index routes under the table:
   /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}/indexes[/{index}], with
   index names unique per table, plus an optional endpoint to list indexes in
   a namespace.
   - Indexes are sub-resources of their table. Renaming a table moves its
   indexes with it, and dropping a table drops its indexes. How the catalog
   removes them is up to the implementation.
   - Multi-table indexes are out of scope.

   access. The read restrictions section should state that read restrictions
   must be applied whether a client reads the table, the index, or both, so an
   index never exposes data the caller could not otherwise see.

   round trips when the table is loaded for reading. But most loads (for
   example, catalog federation and UIs) don't need full index metadata, and
   producing it on every load adds cost. Options discussed: return indexes by
   default, return them only when the client asks (possibly with only index
   names by default), or distinguish read-path loads from metadata-only loads.
   Clients that don't understand indexes can ignore the extra field either way.

body:
Hi guys

I checked the Java side, and it matches what you both described:
- ParqueSchemaUtil.hasIds() returns true if any field at any depth has an
ID, so a file with only top level IDs never uses the name mapping.
- It does the same per file check with ORCSchemaUtil.hasIds().
- Avro already works per field. AvroSchemaUtil.getFieldId() uses the ID in
the file when there is one and falls back to the mapping when there is not.

For the Java change, removing the hasIds() branch won't be enough. When a
path matches, the Parquet and ORC ApplyNameMapping visitors set the ID from
the mapping and overwrite any ID already in the file. They will need to
keep an ID that's already there and only fill in the missing ones.
Otherwise, "never overrides an ID a writer recorded" is not true.

I think the spec should cover a mapped ID that collides with an embedded ID
on another column of the same file. I believe that can happen with an
outdated or hand written mapping, and then two columns resolve to the same
field ID. This case only exists with the per field reading, because today
readers use either IDs or the mapping for the whole file. Maybe we could
make embedded ID wins and the conflicting mapped ID is ignored, so that
column is treated as having no ID. Failing the read would also be fine.
Either way, we should be explicit in the spec.

Something like that in the spec: "These mappings provide fallback field ids
for fields in a data file that do not have a field id. A field id stored in
the data file always takes precedence over the name mapping."

Manu proposed a PR for the spec, I think it makes sense.

Regards
JB

required for any
implementation to be correct. The divergence comes from readers treating
"does this file use field IDs?"
as an all-or-nothing switch for the whole file.

Iceberg writers don't produce files with only some field IDs (so the Delta
behavior is unexpected),
but if a reader encounters one, resolving each field independently, with
the file's ID taking precedence over the mapping, is unambiguous and safe.

The other cases raised are different: they describe a file where two
columns resolve to
the same ID, which is undefined behavior. It is like adding a name mapping
for a file with
columns A, B, C and mapping all three to ID 1 ({A -> 1, B -> 1, C -> 1}).
That is a user error,
not something the spec should require you to check for.

In general we shouldn't tell implementations how to fail when they
encounter an illegal file.

body:
After digging into the history, the per-file reading is the original
intent, and I'm less supportive of widening it.

I ('m the problem, it's me) added the name mapping text in 2021 (#3542
<https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/3542>, #3556
<https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/3556>). The intent was always the
whole file:

*"These mappings provide fallback field ids to be used when a data file
does not contain field id information."*
The use case was files from Hive and other plain Parquet writers that don't
write field IDs at all, which is why the rest of that section talks about
imported data files.

The per-column wording ("map field id to columns without field id") came in
with #10835 <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/10835> in 2024, when we
clarified identity partition values
and initial-default. Name mapping was split into its own resolution step
there, but we weren't trying to change its scope, and partial files weren't
discussed.

Iceberg writers are required to store field IDs for every field, so a file
with only some IDs isn't a valid Iceberg data file. From this thread,
the only source of these files is Delta tables using column mapping without
IcebergCompatV2. Delta only assigns IDs to struct fields,
and IcebergCompatV2 exists specifically to add the missing IDs for list
elements and map keys and values.

So the proposal would change behavior we've had since 2021, based on a
sentence added unintentionally in 2024, to support files from a
Delta configuration that isn't meant to be Iceberg compatible. It also adds
a new requirement for every
implementation (per-field resolution, never overwriting embedded IDs, and
defining what happens on collisions).

I'd rather fix the 2024 sentence to match the original meaning: the name
mapping applies to data files
that don't contain field IDs. If we want name mappings to apply to files
that have only some IDs, I think that's a new feature,
and we should start from the use cases. So far the only one I've seen is
Delta. This may be valid, but let's restart this as a discussion
of a new feature then instead of a spec clarification.

conversion stays under 0.4 s, while random UUID keys on a 10,000-file table
read every file and take 2 to 42 s depending on storage latency. koodin9
agrees a full read is too expensive on large tables, so part 2 would
document the mode for tables that prune well, with an index (#16961 [3]) as
the path for the rest.
- At the Oct 28 community sync [4], nobody argued for dropping upserts from
the sink. The position was to add nothing that produces new equality
deletes.

I went back to the code after the sync, and two things I said there were
off. The mainline sink is append-only today; the upsert mode with equality
deletes was in Tabular's version. And #18003 [5] doesn't convert in a

Hi Kevin,

This is a tough one. Overall, I'm +1 for dropping write support for
Avro and ORC. They are not first class citizens today, and they likely
never will become. The community clearly has chosen Parquet.

That said, we should continue to support multiple file formats (read
and write), and we must continue to support reading Avro and ORC to
retain backwards-compatibility. The primary challenge of only having
one write format is to remain open to other formats in the write path.
This is perhaps the biggest advantage of keeping other formats.

Were you able to test performance under commit contention with other writes
(e.g. compaction)?

Writing deletion vectors instead of equality deletes can generate
significant contention. For delete-heavy low-latency commit workloads like
Kafka Connect CDC, contention can result in many commit retries, increased
latency, and decreased throughput.

in more detail

I don't think it is a good idea to try to mix name mapping and IDs. The
reason why we check hasIds is that the presence of any ID means that the
file was written with IDs and we should trust them. If an ID is missing,
then that column is null.

Name mapping is a fallback for files converted from Hive without any IDs.
The two should not be mixed.

I agree with Russell's conclusion about fixing the changes that we made for
compatibility. But those changes mean that we can move forward without some
IDs, not that we use name mapping to fill them in.

Ryan
